transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. I, um, I guess I'm here because I'm just so incredibly tired. And I know everyone says they're tired, right? Like, "Oh, I didn't sleep well," or "I had a long day," but this isn't like that. This is... it's like a heaviness, you know? It's like I'm walking through molasses. And it doesn't matter how much I sleep. I could sleep for ten hours, twelve hours, and I wake up and I'm still just exhausted. It's not a sleep thing, it's a... I don't know, a whole-body thing. Like, even just the thought of doing normal things is exhausting. The other day, I was looking at the dishwasher, and I knew I needed to unload it, and I just stood there because it felt like climbing a mountain. Just putting plates in a cupboard! And I'm trying to take this certificate class online, you know, since I'm not working right now, just trying to better myself, and I sit down to read the material, and my brain just feels like mush. I can't focus, I can't retain anything, and it just takes so much energy just to look at the screen. It's like my battery is constantly at one percent, and no matter how long I leave it plugged in, it never charges. It's incredibly frustrating because I want to do things, I really do, but I just... I can't seem to find the energy to even start.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you normally like doing?

Yeah, exactly. That's... that's a huge part of it, actually. It's like I've just completely stopped caring about the things that usually make me feel like myself. And I used to have so many things I loved doing! Like, I've always been a really creative person, and I used to sketch all the time. I have this beautiful leather-bound sketchbook that I used to take to the coffee shop, and I'd just sit there for hours drawing people, just getting lost in it. But now it’s just sitting on my nightstand gathering dust, and I don't even have the urge to open it. 

And I used to love going to gallery openings downtown. You know, you get dressed up a little, have a glass of wine, look at the new exhibits, talk to people... it was always such a fun night out. But the last few times I got invites, I just deleted the emails. The thought of going just felt completely pointless. 

And it's not just the going-out stuff, it's the at-home stuff too. Like cooking. I used to really enjoy cooking, looking up new recipes, spending an hour just chopping vegetables and making a really nice meal from scratch. It was relaxing for me. Now? I just open the fridge, look inside, and shut it. I just don't care what I eat. 

Even the active things that usually make me feel good... I used to do yoga a few times a week right in my living room just to center myself, but I haven't unrolled my mat in I don't know how long. I even have this friend I usually play tennis with—we've had this standing Thursday morning thing for months—and I've canceled on her the last three times. I keep making up excuses because I don't know how to explain to her that I just don't care about playing tennis right now. I don't care about any of it. It’s just so frustrating because these are the things that make up my life, you know? And right now I just feel completely blank about all of them.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the time lately?

You know, it's funny you ask it that way, because... no, not really. I mean, when I think of being depressed or feeling down, I think of being really sad, right? Like crying into a pillow, or feeling heartbroken, or watching those sad commercials with the rescue dogs and just bawling your eyes out. But I don't have that at all. I haven't been crying. It's not a sad feeling. It’s more like... well, like I was saying before, it's just this massive blankness. 

So if you mean "down" like sad and weeping, then no, definitely not. I remember when my grandmother passed away a few years ago, I was devastated, just crying every day, feeling this heavy, sharp ache in my chest. That was sadness. This isn't that ache. It's almost like I don't even have the energy to be sad. I actually kept waiting for the tears to come, thinking maybe if I just had a really good cry I'd feel a little bit better, a little lighter? So the other night I even tried putting on this movie, "Steel Magnolias," which usually absolutely destroys me, but... nothing. I just stared at the screen. I knew it was a sad scene, but I didn't feel anything in my chest. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed in that emotional, heavy-hearted way. It's just... flat. Like someone turned the volume all the way down on my emotions and pulled the plug out of the wall. Because my mom keeps calling and asking me, "Honey, are you depressed? You sound depressed," and I keep having to explain to her, "Mom, I'm not sad, I'm just tired and I don't care about anything." It's hard to get people to understand that you can feel absolutely nothing without actually feeling sad. So yeah, I haven't really noticed feeling down most of the time, just... empty.
Have you been feeling like you’re worthless or have been blaming yourself for things more than usual?

No, not really. I mean, I know I'm not working right now, and I guess society sometimes tells you that your worth is tied to your job or how productive you are, but I don't actually feel worthless. It's not like that at all. Like, I know some people get really down on themselves when they can't get things done. I have a friend who went through a rough patch a few years ago, and she was constantly saying she was a burden to her husband and her kids, just really beating herself up over every little thing she didn't do perfectly. But my brain isn't doing that. I don't sit on the couch thinking I'm a terrible person or a failure just because I didn't unload the dishwasher or because I haven't picked up my sketchbook. 

I know I have worth, you know? I know I'm smart and capable—that's why I signed up for that certificate program in the first place, because I know I have the potential to do more and I want to finish my education eventually. When I sit down and stare at the screen and can't focus on the modules, I don't think, "Oh, I'm so stupid, I'm useless." I just think, "Wow, my brain is literally too tired to read this sentence." It's more of a frustration with my physical energy levels than a judgment about who I am as a person. 

And as for blaming myself... no, I don't think so. I mean, sure, I feel a tiny bit bad when I cancel tennis on Thursdays, just because I don't like letting people down and she's a good friend, but I don't agonize over it or think I'm this awful, flaky person who doesn't deserve friends. I just kind of accept that I can't do it right now. I don't think any of this is my fault, really. It just feels like something that's happening to me, like catching a really bad bug, but it's this weird, heavy exhaustion instead of a fever. So I'm definitely not sitting around hating myself or feeling guilty all day. I actually have pretty decent self-esteem, all things considered. I just... I'm just a person who is completely out of gas right now. I know I'm still a good person, I just don't have the energy to do anything about it.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently? Like eating a lot more or less than usual, or gaining or losing weight without trying?

Yeah, actually, I have. Food has just been... well, like I was saying earlier about not cooking anymore, the whole concept of eating just feels like a massive chore. My appetite has been really, really off. I'll wake up and make coffee—I have this French press, so I'll make a whole batch of it and just drink that while I'm sitting around staring at the wall. But then the hours just kind of blur together, you know? And because I'm not really doing anything, I guess I don't feel hungry, or maybe I just don't care enough to notice the hunger. 

So it'll get to be like five or six o'clock in the evening, and I'll suddenly realize that I've literally only had coffee and maybe a few bites of a granola bar or a handful of dry crackers all day long. It's like my stomach just forgot how to tell my brain it needs food. I just have zero interest in it. 

And because of that, yeah, I've definitely lost weight, which is weird because I'm absolutely not trying to. I haven't been stepping on a scale or anything, but the other day I actually had to put on real clothes to run to the drugstore because I was completely out of toothpaste and couldn't put it off anymore. So I put on my favorite pair of jeans. They're these vintage Levi's that usually fit me perfectly, like, really snug right at the waist. But when I buttoned them, they were just sagging. My jeans have gotten so much looser. I actually had to dig through the back of my closet to find a belt just so they wouldn't slide down while I was walking around the store. 

Which, again, is crazy because I'm not dieting, and obviously with the tennis and yoga being totally ignored lately, I'm not exactly burning any extra calories. I'm just kind of shrinking by accident because putting food together and actually chewing and swallowing it just takes more effort than I have to give right now.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep lately, like having trouble falling asleep, waking up a lot during the night, or sleeping much more than usual?

Actually, no. My sleep is... well, it's pretty much the exact same as it's always been. Which is almost frustrating, you know? You'd think with how absolutely drained and heavy I feel all day, like I was describing before, that I'd be sleeping for fourteen hours a day, like a bear in hibernation or something. But I'm not. I still go to bed around eleven or eleven-thirty, which has been my bedtime since I was in my twenties, really. I have this really great memory foam mattress, the kind that kind of sinks in and hugs you? I bought it a couple of years ago, and it usually guarantees a good night's sleep. And it still does, honestly. I fall asleep fine. It's not like I'm tossing and turning or staring at the ceiling with racing thoughts or anything. My brain is way too empty and tired to race. I just close my eyes and I'm out. 

And I sleep right through the night, usually until about seven or seven-thirty, which is a solid eight hours. I don't wake up in the middle of the night at all. It's just that when I wake up... I don't feel rested. Like, I'll hear the garbage trucks outside—they always come on Tuesdays and Fridays right around 7:15, and they are incredibly loud, so that usually wakes me up—but I just lie there. I don't go back to sleep, I just don't have the drive to actually get up. So I might stay in bed for another hour or two, just staring at the wall or watching the light change in the room, but I'm not actually sleeping more than usual. I'm just horizontal. 

And I'm not taking naps during the day either, even though I'm sitting on the couch doing nothing. I'll just sit there. It's like I'm completely exhausted, but my body's sleep switch is still on its normal factory settings. So yeah, no real changes with the actual sleeping part, I'm not sleeping more or less, and I'm not having trouble falling asleep. It's just the getting out of bed part that's different.
Have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself or not wanting to be alive?

Oh, no. No, definitely not. I know people get to that point when they are feeling really low, and I have read about it, but that is just not where my head is at all. Like, I was sitting on the couch the other day, this was maybe Wednesday or Thursday, and I was looking out the front window. My neighbor was out there walking his golden retriever, and I was just watching them. I remember thinking to myself that I really wish I had the energy to go outside and walk a dog or just feel the sun on my face. I want to be doing those things. I want to be participating in life, you know? 

So it is not that I do not want to be alive. It is almost the exact opposite. I want to be alive and doing things, but my body is just... it is like it is made of wet sand right now. I am just so incredibly heavy and drained all the time. But I would never hurt myself. I am actually really squeamish about pain, to be completely honest with you. I cannot even watch those medical dramas on television because the sight of blood or needles just completely grosses me out and makes me lightheaded. I remember when I had to get blood drawn for a routine physical a few years ago, I almost passed out just sitting in the waiting room chair before they even brought the needle out. 

So hurting myself is completely off the table. And as for not wanting to be here, I really do want to be here. I want to finish that certificate program I was telling you about earlier. I want to get back to playing tennis on Thursdays with my friend. I want to actually enjoy my French press coffee instead of just using the mug as a hand warmer while I stare at the wall for hours. I just want this weird, heavy exhaustion to lift so I can get back to being me and doing my normal routine. But yeah, no dark thoughts like that at all. I am just sort of waiting for my battery to recharge, I guess.
Have you had any periods in the past where you felt significantly better for at least two months, where these symptoms weren't present?

Two whole months? No... no, I really don't think so. I mean, when I try to think back to when I felt completely normal, like my old self—you know, actually working on my certificate program and keeping up with things without feeling like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight around—I just can't pinpoint a solid block of time like that. 

It feels like this has just been dragging on forever. I was actually looking at the calendar on my phone the other day, because I use this app that color-codes everything. Like, I use blue for appointments, and green for social stuff, which is basically totally empty right now, obviously. But I was scrolling back through the months, just trying to figure out when exactly this whole slump started, or if there was a break in it, and it all just blends together into this one long, gray stretch. 

It's not like there was a magic Tuesday where I woke up and everything was great for eight weeks straight. I mean, sure, there might be a random afternoon where I think, "Okay, maybe I can manage a quick trip to the grocery store today," or I'll manage to answer an email, but then the very next morning I'm right back on the couch staring at the wall with my cold French press coffee. 

So a full two months of feeling significantly better, where none of this heavy feeling was happening? No, absolutely not. It's just been this continuous, slow crawl for a long time now. Even when we had that really nice stretch of weather a while back, I thought maybe that would snap me out of it, because usually I love sitting out on the patio and just enjoying the breeze, but... no. It just hasn't lifted for anywhere near that long. It's just been a constant, steady drain.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the heaviness, loss of interest, and lack of energy?

Well, let me think... if I really trace it back, this whole quiet, depressed stretch has been going on for about three months now. Yeah, three months. I know this because, well, I mentioned my phone calendar earlier, but I also keep a physical planner. I'm a bit old-school like that, I just love the feeling of actually writing things down with a good pen. I buy these specific notebooks online that have the really thick paper, you know, where the ink doesn't bleed through to the other side? I'm very particular about it. 

Anyway, I was looking at it recently, and the entries just sort of... stop. Like, I was writing down my tennis days and my study goals for the certificate program, making my little to-do lists, and then right around three months ago, it just goes completely blank. Nothing but white space week after week. And that lines up perfectly with when this heavy fatigue really set in and took over. 

It hasn't been, like, a dramatic, crying-all-the-time type of thing, just this very quiet, heavy stretch where my interest in literally everything just completely vanished. So it's been about three solid months of just feeling like I'm dragging myself through wet cement. Which is honestly so frustrating to even say out loud, because three months is a really long time! That's a whole quarter of a year. People learn new languages or train for half-marathons in three months, and I've just been sitting on my couch watching the dust motes float around in the living room light, completely drained of any energy or interest in participating in my own life. But yes, looking at the blank pages and just how long I've been stuck like this, it's been right around the three-month mark.

Have you experienced a time in the last three months when you felt absolutely no emotional response to things that used to bring you joy, like your sketching, cooking, or social events, even when they were happening around you?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It is exactly like that, and it is honestly one of the strangest parts of this whole thing. It is like someone just flipped a switch and all the color completely drained out of everything. 

I mean, I stopped caring about the things that usually make me feel like myself, which is so unsettling. Take my sketching, for example. I have always been such a visual person, and I usually carry this little charcoal sketchbook with me everywhere—it is this specific brand that fits right in my purse, and I usually love just sitting at a cafe and capturing people's expressions or drawing the architecture. But lately? I look at my pencils sitting on the desk and I just feel... nothing. Zero spark. 

And it is the same with going out. A friend invited me to this gallery opening downtown a few weeks ago. Usually, I absolutely live for that kind of thing, you know? Looking at new mixed-media pieces, chatting with the local artists, even just dressing up a little and walking around the exhibits. I actually forced myself to go, thinking maybe it would help, but I was just standing there in the middle of the room, surrounded by all this vibrant art and people laughing, and I felt completely blank. The canvases could have been blank white walls for all I cared. I just had no emotional reaction to any of it.

And it is not just art stuff, either. It is literally everything. Like cooking! I usually love spending a whole Sunday afternoon trying out a new, complicated recipe, chopping all the vegetables perfectly, getting all the spices measured out in those cute little glass prep bowls I bought last year. But now, the thought of even boiling water for pasta feels entirely pointless. I just don't care about food or the process of making it. 

Same with my yoga practice. I have this really nice, extra-thick mat because the hardwood floors in my apartment are pretty tough on my knees, and I used to do a flow every single morning to center myself. Now the mat is just rolled up in the corner collecting dust, and I look at it and feel totally indifferent. And I know I mentioned my Thursday tennis matches earlier. My friend keeps texting me to see if I'm ready to get back on the court, and I just... I don't even have the desire to swing a racket. It is not just the physical heaviness I was telling you about, though that is definitely there, but it is this total lack of caring. I just stopped caring about all of it. It is so bizarre because I know in my head that I love these things, but in my chest, there is just no reaction at all. It is just completely flat.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt this same kind of heaviness, loss of interest, and lack of energy for at least two weeks?

Before this? Um... no. No, definitely not. And I say that with absolute certainty because, honestly, if I had ever felt like this before, I think I would have remembered it vividly. It’s just so completely foreign to how I usually operate. 

I mean, sure, I’ve had periods where I was sad or stressed out, obviously. Everyone has bad days. Like, I remember a few years ago when I was taking some early prerequisite classes at the community college—this was way before I started my current certificate program—and I completely bombed this huge biology midterm. I had studied so hard for it, too. I was at the campus library until midnight for like three nights in a row, using all my different colored highlighters, making these incredibly detailed flashcards on those thick index cards I like. And then I got the test back and it was just a total disaster. I was devastated. I went home, crawled into bed, and just cried and ate terrible junk food for like two days straight. I felt so defeated and sluggish and I didn't want to talk to anyone. 

But the thing is, that lasted for exactly one weekend. By Monday morning, I was right back in class, sitting in the front row with my notebook open, figuring out how to get extra credit and talking to the professor. I bounced back. I always bounce back. 

So the idea of feeling this... this absolute heavy, empty drain for two whole weeks, or even longer, at any point in my life before now? No, it’s never happened. That’s actually a big part of why this whole three-month stretch has been so incredibly confusing and, frankly, kind of terrifying for me. Because I’ve always been someone who shakes things off. Usually, I'm the one dragging my friends out of the house when they're having a bad week, not the other way around. I’ve just never experienced anything even close to this kind of prolonged, heavy slump before in my entire life. So, no, definitely not.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt this same kind of heaviness, loss of interest, and lack of energy for at least two weeks?

I know I just went on a whole tangent about my biology midterm, but just to be absolutely clear—no, never. I've really been racking my brain while we're sitting here, trying to think if there was *any* time, maybe in my twenties, where I felt anything even close to this for two weeks, and I just haven't. 

Like, when I was twenty-four, I took a year off from school and worked at this little boutique downtown. They sold these amazing handmade soaps and imported candles—the whole shop constantly smelled like lavender and cedarwood, and I was in charge of arranging all the window displays, which I took very seriously. It was actually a really lovely place to work, but I was definitely stressed about money and figuring out my life path back then. I didn't know what I wanted to major in, my rent was going up, and I was definitely having a bit of a quarter-life crisis. 

But even then, feeling lost or stressed wasn't anything like this heavy, empty feeling I have now. I still had energy back then. I still cared. I'd still go out with my coworkers after our shifts, and we'd grab food and complain about the rude customers or talk about our plans for the weekend. I was still sketching, I was still going for runs. So even during the most transitional, uncertain times in my life, I never, ever had a two-week period where I just couldn't get off the couch or lost interest in my own life. It really has strictly been these past three months. Before this, my baseline was always just so much more active and engaged, which is exactly why this whole experience feels so completely wrong and jarring to me. So, yeah, to answer your question again, definitely not.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt this same kind of heaviness, loss of interest, and lack of energy for at least two weeks?

I... wait, didn't you just ask me that? I feel like we're going in circles a bit here, doctor. But, um, just to reiterate, no. Never. 

I promise I'm not hiding anything or, you know, forgetting some big chunk of my past. I really, truly have never felt this way before these last three months. You know, I've always been the kind of person who just... keeps moving. Even when I was a teenager, which is usually when everyone is supposed to be super moody and locking themselves in their rooms and ignoring the world, right? I was never like that. I had this bright yellow bedroom—my dad painted it for me when I was twelve, the color was literally called 'sunflower burst' or something ridiculous like that, I picked it out myself at the hardware store—and I was always in there organizing my things, listening to CDs, planning out my week. I was just such an active kid. 

So if I had ever had a two-week stretch where I felt like a lead weight and didn't care about anything, my parents would have noticed immediately. My mom especially, she was always hovering, always asking if I was eating enough or sleeping enough, you know how moms can be. If I had stayed in bed for two weeks back then, or stopped caring about my friends, she probably would have dragged me to the emergency room herself! But that never happened. I went to school, I hung out with my friends, I did my chores. 

So, I don't know if I'm not explaining it right, or if you're looking for a specific answer, but I really have to say no again. This current slump is the absolute first time in my thirty-three years of life that I've experienced this kind of total shutdown. I swear.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt down, lost interest in things, or had low energy for at least two weeks?

I... I'm sorry, I feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here. Are you... are you asking me the exact same question again? I mean, I know I talk a lot, I know I tend to ramble and give you my whole life story when you probably just want a yes or no, but... did I not answer this? 

I really, truly, honestly mean it when I say no. No, I have never, ever felt like this before. Not for two weeks, not for one week. This heavy, awful, exhausting feeling where I just don't care about anything and can't find the energy to even make a cup of tea... it is completely new. It started three months ago, and before that, it just wasn't a thing in my life. 

I don't know how else to explain it, doctor. I've told you about my college classes, I told you about my twenties working at the soap shop, I told you about my bright yellow bedroom when I was a teenager... I've gone through every phase of my life in my head just now, and there is just no precedent for this. I've always been the energetic one. I've always been the one doing things. So... no. Never before this. I promise. I really don't know what else to say.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this one where you felt down, lost interest in things, or had low energy for at least two weeks?

Okay, wait, I... I feel like I'm being pranked right now. Are you... is this some sort of psychological test? Like, are you trying to see if I'll change my answer if you ask me enough times? Because I really, truly don't know what you want me to say. 

I mean, I'm sitting here, and I'm trying to be as cooperative as possible, and I'm answering you as honestly as I can. I've told you about my whole life, basically. I've told you about my childhood, my twenties, the soap shop, the yellow bedroom, my mom hovering over me... I mean, I've literally laid it all out there. And the answer is still no. It's just no. 

I've never had a period of two weeks where I felt like this. Not ever. Not when I was a teenager, not when I was in my twenties, not ever. This current situation, these past three months, this is the absolute first time I've ever experienced anything like this. This complete lack of energy, this total loss of interest in everything, this heaviness... it's all brand new. 

I don't know how else to convince you. I feel like I'm on trial or something, and I'm just repeating the same testimony over and over. Am I supposed to suddenly remember some secret hidden depression from ten years ago? Because I don't have one. I've always been the active person. I've always been the one doing things. So, for the fourth time, or however many times we've done this now... no. Never. I promise. I swear on my life. No.
Have you had any periods in the last three months where your symptoms improved significantly for at least two weeks, even if they came back afterward?

No, no, definitely not. I wish there had been a break, I really do, but... no. It's just been one long, unbroken blur. Like I was saying before, this whole... this quieter, depressed stretch I've been in, with the completely low interest in everything and that heavy, heavy fatigue that just weighs down my arms and legs... it has been going on for about three months straight. 

There hasn't been any sort of two-week window where the clouds parted or anything like that. It's funny you ask about two weeks, because I remember when it first started, I kept thinking, 'Okay, maybe next week I'll snap out of it, maybe I just need to rest for a few days.' But the days just kept stacking up. I'd look at the calendar in the kitchen—the one with the little pictures of national parks that my aunt got me—and I'd see whole weeks gone by where I hadn't done a single thing. Month one passed, then month two, and I was still just too exhausted to even care about making a proper meal or calling anyone back. 

So, no, there hasn't been any improvement or bouncing back, not even for a few days. It's just been a solid three months of this same heavy, quiet slump, day in and day out, without any breaks at all.

Before these past three months, have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt down or lost interest in things, even if it was shorter or less intense than what you're experiencing now?

Okay... I... I really don't know what is happening right now. Are you reading off a clipboard that just has the exact same question written five different ways? Because, doctor, I swear to you, the answer hasn't changed. Not even for a "less intense" version. 

Before these last three months, my life was just... it was completely different. I wasn't down. I wasn't losing interest in things. I didn't have "less intense" slumps. If I was sad, it was because, I don't know, a movie was sad or I had a silly argument with my mom about my life choices, and it lasted for like, a day. A few hours, maybe. Not two weeks. Never two weeks. 

I was always the one who was on the go. You know, when I was taking those college classes I told you about, I was the one organizing the study groups, keeping everybody talking, staying busy... I wasn't hiding in my bed. I just didn't do "down." It wasn't in my vocabulary until three months ago. I feel like I'm taking crazy pills here, having to say this yet again, but I really, truly, absolutely mean it. I am searching my brain, looking at every single year of my thirty-three years on this planet, and there is just nothing there. No. Nothing. Zero prior times. Not even a little bit.
